Chapter 11 · Example 11.3

[0,1] Game #2 the half-street game with folding — von Neumann's poker model, made live

Half a street, one bet. X must check in the dark; then Y may bet or check, and if Y bets, X may call or fold. Hands are uniform on [0, 1] (0 = the nuts). Because X can now fold, Y starts to bluff — and the whole betting/bluffing/calling balance is governed by one number, the pot size P. This is the ancestor of Games #9–#11.

Historical note. This is essentially the poker model John von Neumann & Oskar Morgenstern solved in Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944) — one of the first games ever solved by game theory. Chen & Ankenman recast it as [0,1] Game #2.

Value of the game to Y  vs. pot

Ex-showdown expectation to Y: G = (1−α)² / [2(2−α)(1+α)]. It rises from 0 (tiny pot, no betting) toward ¼ as P→∞ — exactly the no-fold Game #1 value. The dot marks the current pot.

How to read it

Y bets his best hands for value [0, y₁], checks the middle [y₁, y₀], and bluffs his worst [y₀, 1]. X calls his best [0, x₁*] and folds the rest. The one lever is α = 1/(P+1).

Bluffs and value bets balance at ratio α (1−y₀ = α·y₁), and X folds α of the hands that could beat a bluff — each side making the other exactly indifferent. This is the α that runs through every later game.

Bet half of what gets called. The calling cutoff is x₁* = 2y₁ — Y value-bets exactly half the hands X will call with. And there'd be no bluffing without folding: if Y only value-bet, X would fold everything weak and Y couldn't get paid, so Y must bluff to drag X's calls down to [y₁, x₁*].

The value of position. Being the player who gets to bet is worth G per hand — from 0 in a vanishing pot up to ¼ of a bet in an enormous one. That ¼ is the pure value of the betting lead when folding no longer matters.

Model & solution from Bill Chen & Jerrod Ankenman, The Mathematics of Poker, Example 11.3 (“[0,1] Game #2”), with the game value from Chapter 18 (Eq. 18.1). Exact closed forms: α=1/(P+1), y₁=(1−α)/[(2−α)(1+α)], x₁*=2y₁, y₀=1−αy₁, G=y₁(1−α)/2. Originally von Neumann & Morgenstern (1944). Companion to game9.html, game10.html, game11.html.
